title: Do I Need an Audio Interface for a Digital Piano?
seo_title: Do I Need an Audio Interface for a Digital Piano?
description: Do you need an audio interface for a digital piano? A concert pianist explains when USB or a cable is enough, and when an interface is worth buying.
sub: Most adults do not need one. Here is how to tell, and which three I would look at if you do.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: Forty-one lessons in order, free, at your own pace:
body:
By Dr. Maria Pisarenko, DMA · Last updated: November 16, 2026 · Product details checked against the Amazon listing and the maker's page on that date or on November 14, 2026.

You do not need an audio interface to play a digital piano, to hear it through headphones, or to use it with most piano apps. You need one when you want to record the piano's sound with good quality, or to add a microphone, and your piano cannot send audio over its own USB cable. If you only want to practice, stop here and save your money.

As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. That never changes what I recommend: every item here is something I would tell my own adult students to look at. Check today's price on Amazon.

My top 3 picks

  • Simplest: Focusrite Scarlett Solo 4th Gen — one microphone preamp and a line input for the piano
  • Most room to grow: Audient EVO 4 — two microphone preamps, so a stereo pair fits
  • If you own MIDI gear: Arturia MiniFuse 2 — a USB audio and MIDI interface

How I choose

The question is not which interface is best. It is whether you need one at all, so I start with what you want to do, and only then with the box. I have not played every instrument or used every device in this guide, and I do not say that I have. What I give you is what I look for as a concert pianist who teaches adults, checked against what each Amazon listing and manufacturer page actually states.

What an audio interface actually does

An audio interface is a small box that turns sound into a signal your computer can record, and turns the computer's signal back into sound for your headphones. It has inputs for microphones and instruments, a headphone output, and a USB cable to the computer. A digital piano already makes its own sound, so for a piano with a line output or a headphone jack, an interface is the clean way to get that sound into a recording program.

When you do not need one

  • You only practice. Headphones plugged into the piano are enough.
  • You use a piano app or notation software. USB carries MIDI, which tells the software which notes you played. Many pianos have a computer USB port; Roland lists one on the FP-10, and Casio lists USB Type A and Type B ports on the CDP-S360. See how to connect a digital piano to a computer.
  • Your piano sends audio over USB. Yamaha lists a 24-bit stereo USB audio interface on the P-225, which means a single cable can carry the piano's sound into a recording program. Check your manual for the same feature on your model.

When you do

  • You want to record the sound, and your piano has no USB audio. Run a cable from the piano's line output into an interface.
  • You want to record a microphone, for your voice or for an acoustic piano. A microphone needs a preamp, and an interface has one.
  • You want to record a second instrument or a stereo pair of microphones. You then need two microphone inputs. Read the best audio interface for beginners.

What I would look at, in order

First, the number of microphone preamps: one is enough for a digital piano's line output and a voice; two are needed for a stereo pair. Second, whether the headphone output is clear and quiet, because you will listen to your own playing on it. Third, whether it runs from the computer's USB cable, so there is no power brick. After those, I do not care about the feature list. A student who finds the box simple will record more often, and recording yourself is how you hear what your teacher would hear.

Focusrite Scarlett Solo 4th Gen

Who it is for: A pianist who records one microphone, or the stereo line from a digital piano, and wants a simple box.

What the listing says: Focusrite lists one microphone preamp, one instrument input and one line input, two balanced line outputs, one headphone output, 24-bit/192 kHz converters, phantom power, loopback, Air mode, USB-C bus power, and software including Ableton Live Lite, Pro Tools Intro+ and Cubase LE. Its spec page does not list MIDI.

What I look for: A clean, quiet recording of a piano starts with a quiet preamp and an honest headphone output. I look at how simple the front panel is: the fewer decisions between the piano and the file, the more often a student will actually record.

The simplest answer for most adults, and the one I would suggest for a digital piano's line output.

Cons
  • One microphone preamp, so a stereo pair of microphones does not fit
  • No MIDI listed on the specification page

Buy it if you record one microphone or the line out of a digital piano. Skip it if you want two microphones at once for a stereo piano recording.

faq: Do I need an audio interface to record my digital piano?
Not always. If your piano sends audio over USB you can record with one cable. If it does not, an interface lets you record its line output cleanly.
Do I need an audio interface for MIDI?
No. MIDI travels over a USB cable on most digital pianos, and the computer reads it directly.
Is a USB microphone a substitute?
For a voice, often yes. For a stereo recording of a piano, an interface with two preamps and two microphones gives you more control.

title: How to Record a Digital Piano Without a Microphone

body:
By Dr. Maria Pisarenko, DMA · Last updated: November 16, 2026 · Product details checked against the Amazon listing and the maker's page on that date or on November 14, 2026.

You can record a digital piano without a microphone in three ways: over USB if the piano sends audio, with a cable from its output into an audio interface, or, for a quick practice take, by playing the sound through a phone's recorder. The first two give you the piano's own sound with none of the room in it, which is often what you want when you are checking notes and rhythm.

  • Simplest cable setup: Focusrite Scarlett Solo 4th Gen — a line input and a headphone output in one small box
  • Lowest cost: Behringer UMC22 — a 2-in 2-out USB interface
  • Most flexible: Audient EVO 4 — two microphone preamps if you add microphones later

How I choose

A piano is sound before it is anything else, so I choose the route that keeps the piano's sound clean and the steps few. The fewer the steps, the more often a student actually records. I have not played every instrument or used every device in this guide, and I do not say that I have. What I give you is what I look for as a concert pianist who teaches adults, checked against what each Amazon listing and manufacturer page actually states.

Why record without a microphone at all?

A microphone records the piano and everything near it: the room, the chair, the kettle in the next room. A digital piano's output carries only the instrument. For an adult learning alone this is an advantage. You hear your touch, your timing and your wrong notes without anything softening them, and that is the point of recording yourself. If you later want the sound of a room, that is a different tool; I cover it in how to record an acoustic piano with two microphones.

Way 1: USB audio

Some digital pianos send their sound over the USB cable as well as MIDI. Yamaha lists a 24-bit stereo USB audio interface on the P-225, for example, so one cable to your computer can carry the sound into a free recording program. Check your piano's manual for the words USB audio, not just USB MIDI. If the manual says MIDI only, the cable will tell the computer which notes you played but will not carry the sound.

Way 2: a cable to an audio interface

If your piano has a line output or a headphone output, you can run a cable from it to an interface and plug the interface into the computer. Use the line output if there is one, because the headphone output is shaped for headphones and can sound a little harsh when recorded. Focusrite lists one instrument input and one line input on the Scarlett Solo, which is why I suggest it here, and the interface's headphone output lets you listen without a delay. If you have never connected a piano to a computer, read how to connect a digital piano to a computer first.

Way 3: a phone for a quick take

For a practice take that only you will hear, a phone's voice recorder held near the piano's speakers will do. It will not sound like a recording, but it will tell you whether your left hand came in on time. If you want to send me a recording for feedback, the free route on my site is the submit page.

What to listen for in your recording

  • Evenness. Are the notes of a scale the same volume? Uneven notes mean uneven fingers.
  • Rhythm. Are the long notes held to their full length? Count aloud as you listen.
  • Pedal. Does the sound blur where the harmony changes?

title: How to Record an Acoustic Piano with Two Microphones
seo_title: How to Record an Acoustic Piano with Two Microphones
description: How to record an acoustic piano in stereo with two microphones: the gear you need, where to place them, and what to listen for, from a concert pianist.
sub: Two matched microphones and a two-input interface give a piano its width. Here is the setup and the first placement to try.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: Forty-one lessons in order, free, at your own pace:
body:
By Dr. Maria Pisarenko, DMA · Last updated: November 16, 2026 · Product details checked against the Amazon listing and the maker's page on that date or on November 14, 2026.

To record an acoustic piano in stereo you need two matching small-diaphragm condenser microphones, two stands, two XLR cables and an audio interface with two microphone preamps and phantom power. Put the pair a little above the strings, pointing at the hammers, listen on headphones, and move them until the middle of the piano sounds like a piano and not like a box.

As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. That never changes what I recommend: every item here is something I would tell my own adult students to look at. Check today's price on Amazon.

My top 3 picks

  • A first matched pair: RODE M5 matched pair — small-diaphragm cardioid condensers, XLR
  • Listed for pianos: sE Electronics sE7 matched pair — a stereo pair the listing names for pianos
  • Interface with two preamps: Focusrite Scarlett 2i2 4th Gen — the box to plug a pair into

How I choose

A stereo piano recording is a listening problem more than a gear problem. I start with a matched pair and a quiet room, and I trust my ears over any chart. I have not played every instrument or used every device in this guide, and I do not say that I have. What I give you is what I look for as a concert pianist who teaches adults, checked against what each Amazon listing and manufacturer page actually states.

What you need

  • Two microphones of the same model. A matched pair has the same character on both sides, which a stereo image needs.
  • An interface with two microphone preamps and phantom power. Condenser microphones need phantom power. Focusrite lists two microphone preamps and phantom power on the Scarlett 2i2, and Audient lists two on the EVO 4. A one-preamp box cannot do this.
  • Two stands and two XLR cables. See stands and accessories.
  • Headphones that let you hear what the microphones hear: headphones for practice.

Where to put them

There is no single right place, and any numbers in a magazine are a starting point, not a rule. I begin with the lid up, the microphones a little above the strings and pointing down toward the hammers, one nearer the treble and one nearer the bass, and far enough back that I can hear the whole piano and not just the loudest strings. Then I play a slow chord progression, listen on headphones, and move one microphone at a time. If the bass booms, move back. If the treble is sharp, move out of line with the hammers.

Check the middle of the piano

The most common beginner mistake is a hole in the middle: the bass on the left, the treble on the right, and nothing between. Play a scale up the keyboard and listen for whether the sound travels smoothly from left to right. If it jumps, bring the microphones closer together or farther back. This is also where a matched pair earns its keep.

The room matters as much as the microphones

A bare room adds echo that no interface can remove. Soft furniture, curtains and a rug help more than a more expensive microphone. If you can, record when the house is quiet, and turn off anything that hums. For a first recording, my guide to a home recording corner on a budget shows what to change first.

What if I only want a simple recording?

A handheld stereo recorder is easier; read the best handheld recorder for piano practice. For a longer list of microphones, see the best pair of microphones for piano.

title: How to Use a MIDI Keyboard with a Laptop or iPad
seo_title: How to Use a MIDI Keyboard with a Laptop or iPad
description: How to connect a MIDI keyboard to a laptop or iPad, which cable and adapter you may need, and what software to use, explained by a concert pianist.
sub: A MIDI keyboard makes no sound on its own. Here is how to connect one to a laptop or an iPad, and which keyboard I would choose.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: Forty-one lessons in order, free, at your own pace:
body:
By Dr. Maria Pisarenko, DMA · Last updated: November 16, 2026 · Product details checked against the Amazon listing and the maker's page on that date or on November 14, 2026.

To use a MIDI keyboard with a laptop you usually need only the USB cable that comes with it. With an iPad you need the right adapter for the iPad's port, or a keyboard that connects by Bluetooth. Either way the keyboard sends notes to an app or program, and the app makes the sound. A MIDI keyboard on its own is silent.

As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. That never changes what I recommend: every item here is something I would tell my own adult students to look at. Check today's price on Amazon.

My top 3 picks

  • Best touch for a pianist: M-Audio Hammer 88 — 88 weighted hammer-action keys, no sound of its own
  • Lower-cost 88 keys: M-Audio Keystation 88 MK3 — 88 semi-weighted keys for apps and software
  • Compact desk keyboard: Arturia KeyLab Essential 49 mk3 — 49 keys for software and apps

How I choose

A MIDI keyboard has no sound of its own, so what I judge is the keys, because the keys are what you will practice on. The software can change tomorrow; your hands will remember the touch. I have not played every instrument or used every device in this guide, and I do not say that I have. What I give you is what I look for as a concert pianist who teaches adults, checked against what each Amazon listing and manufacturer page actually states.

What MIDI is, in one paragraph

MIDI is not sound. It is a message that says which key you pressed, how hard and for how long. The computer or tablet reads those messages and plays a piano sound it already holds. That is why a MIDI keyboard is called a controller, and why it needs software or an app. My guide weighted vs semi-weighted keys explains why the keys matter for a pianist.

With a laptop

  1. Plug the keyboard's USB cable into the laptop. Most laptops recognize it with no driver.
  2. Open the app or program you want to play, and check its settings for the MIDI input. Choose your keyboard.
  3. Play a note. If you hear nothing, check that the program has a piano sound loaded and that the laptop's volume is up.

With an iPad

  1. Check the iPad's port. Some have USB-C and need only a USB-C cable; older ones use a Lightning port and need an adapter.
  2. If the keyboard needs more power than the iPad can give, use a powered adapter or a powered USB hub.
  3. Open your app and choose the keyboard as the MIDI input.

I have not listed the exact adapter for each iPad here, because the right one depends on your iPad and your keyboard; check Apple's page for your model before you buy.

Which software should I use?

Start with a free program. Many piano-learning apps, notation programs and recording programs accept a MIDI keyboard. If you are learning from my free 41-lesson course, you do not need software at all; a MIDI keyboard becomes useful when you want to record yourself or use an app to practice reading notes.

Which keyboard should I buy?

If you want to learn piano repertoire on it, choose 88 keys with a weighted action. If you want a small desk keyboard for software only, 49 keys will do. A 25-key keyboard is a toy for a pianist; it is for sound design, not for learning to play. If a keyboard that makes its own sound is better for you, read the best 88-key weighted MIDI controller and my digital piano guide for adult beginners.

How I choose

Headphones are what you hear your own touch through, so I look at comfort first, then whether the middle of the sound is clear, then whether the bass is steady, and last at whether the leakage is low. Why closed-back?

Open-back headphones let sound pass through the earcups. They can sound airy, but they let the sound out and the room in, which defeats the purpose if you practice at night, in an apartment, or with other people in the house. Closed-back headphones seal the sound in. On a digital piano, that means the piano is the only thing you hear, and nobody else hears it. If you live in a small space, read how to practice piano in an apartment.

What I look for

  • Comfort for an hour. You will wear them for as long as a lesson.
  • A clear middle. A piano's melody lives there. Headphones that scoop the middle make the melody harder to follow.
  • Steady bass. Boomy bass makes you play the left hand too softly.
  • Whether your piano can drive them. A high-impedance pair can sound quiet from a piano's headphone jack. A lower figure, such as the 48 ohms in the DT 770 Pro X listing, is easier to drive.

Put the headphones on and play something slow that you know well, such as a hymn or the first piece in your course. Listen for three things.
